screens.title: Project 5 — The Assembler
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build an assembler that reads Hack assembly language and produces Hack machine code. This is the first software project in the course and it matters because you will write a program that creates programs — a small but powerful form of compilation. The assembler accepts a. asm file, resolves labels and variables, and writes a. hack file with 16-bit binary instructions. Practically speaking, you will implement a parser to break each line into instruction fields, a symbol table to map names to addresses, and a code module to translate mnemonics into bit patterns. You will test on small programs like Add and larger stress tests like Pong, which reveals subtle bugs that small tests miss. By completing this project you learn how human-readable instructions map to machine-level encodings and why two passes—one to record labels and one to translate instructions—are a reliable approach. Think about how a program that writes programs changes your role: you become a builder of tools that create behavior on different hardware. What will your assembler reveal when you run Pong?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter: Project 5 › Overview
Build the Hack Assembler
A lab walkthrough that takes you from spec to tested tool.

You will implement a command-line assembler that accepts a .asm file and emits a .hack file. The project teaches parsing, symbol management, bit-level encoding, and robust testing. This tool is the first program you write in this course that manipulates other programs as data.

In this lesson
Walk through the assembler spec, module structure, two-pass algorithm, code mapping, and practical testing on Add, Max, Rect, and Pong.
Spec
Input .asm → output .hack; 16-bit lines; handle labels and variables.
Implementation
Parser, SymbolTable, and Code modules. Python recommended for concise handling.
Testing
Start with Add, then Max, Rect, and finish with Pong as a stress test.
Tool flow
Assembler (your program) → .hack file → Hack CPU executes.
Implement this flow repeatedly as you test on small then large programs. Each successful run demonstrates that your assembler maps textual instructions to the exact 16-bit encodings the Hack hardware expects.
Explore Key Topics
Parsing
Split lines, ignore comments, classify A/C/L instructions.
Symbol Table
Remember label addresses and allocate variables starting at RAM[16].
Testing
Compare your .hack output with reference files; use Pong to pressure-test correctness.

screens.title: Skills and verification
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to the code you write, verification is essential. Learn how to compare your assembler's output against reference. hack files line-by-line and how to interpret mismatches. You will learn to trace differences by mapping a binary line back to the original assembly: locate the instruction, check symbol resolution, and confirm comp/dest/jump encodings. This objective teaches practical debugging habits: isolate whether a mismatch stems from label address off-by-one, variable allocation starting address, missing predefined symbols, or incorrect parsing of whitespace and comments. Being able to explain why a failing test fails is the difference between a passing run and a robust tool. You will also learn to document the modules in your assembler and to present a short report showing tests passed, remaining issues, and the strategies used to find bugs.

screens.title: What is an assembler?
screens.narratorSegment: An assembler is a program that converts assembly language into machine code. For Project 5 you will implement a Hack assembler that reads human-readable mnemonics and symbolic names and writes 16-bit binary instructions the Hack C P U can execute. Conceptually, the assembler maps textual constructs to fixed-width encodings: an A-instruction becomes a single 16-bit value with the high bit zero and the address in the remaining bits; a C-instruction is encoded with a three-bit prefix, a comp field, dest bits, and jump bits. This translation is precise and unforgiving: a single wrong bit changes behavior. A concrete example is an A-instruction with a numeric address like @17, which should become the 16-bit binary representation of 17. A common misconception is that an assembler merely performs text replacement; instead it must parse, resolve symbols, allocate addresses for variables, and consult translation tables for comp/dest/jump. The key takeaway is that the assembler is the simplest compiler: it implements lexical and syntactic recognition at a small scale and produces exact bit patterns. When you finish this module, ask yourself: how does your symbol resolution strategy ensure labels point to the correct ROM address?

keyIdea.text: Converts textual instructions and symbols into exact 16-bit machine encodings; more than simple text substitution.

content.html:
Module 4 › Assembler Concept › Definition
Definition and claim
An assembler translates assembly into machine code; it parses, resolves symbols, and encodes instructions.
  • • A-instruction: address value encoded as 16-bit binary with high bit 0.
  • • C-instruction: encoded with 111 prefix + comp + dest + jump bits.
  • • Labels allocate ROM addresses during the first pass, variables during the second pass starting at RAM[16].
Analogy
Think of the assembler as a translator that knows both languages: human mnemonics and machine bit patterns.
Concrete example
Assembly: @17 → Machine: 0000000000010001
Misconception
It is not enough to replace names with numbers. The assembler must parse instruction fields, handle whitespace, ignore comments, and perform two passes to handle forward label references.
Key Takeaway
An assembler must both understand structure and produce exact bits; build tests that check both parsing and encoding.

screens.title: Project specification and command line
screens.narratorSegment: Project 5 specifies a simple but exact interface: your assembler must accept a single command-line argument — the name of a. asm file — and produce an output file with the same base name and a. hack extension. Each line in the output file represents a single 16-bit instruction as a string of 0s and 1s. Why this matters: strict input/output contracts let test harnesses run your program automatically and compare outputs precisely. A common execution pattern is to invoke the assembler with a program name, open the. asm file, then write lines to the. hack file in order. A frequent pitfall is not handling file naming edge cases or failing to strip comments and blank lines before translation, which shifts ROM addresses. A concrete practice is to run your assembler on Add. asm and compare the produced Add. hack line-for-line with the reference. If the first differing line is at address 10, trace how you computed addresses up to that point. Remember that the spec requires handling A-instructions, C-instructions, labels, and variables. Before moving on, confirm your program opens files, iterates clean lines, and writes 16-character binary strings for every instruction.

keyIdea.title: Follow the spec exactly
keyIdea.text: A strict CLI and exact file format are necessary for automated testing and correct ROM addressing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Spec & CLI › Project Requirements
Command-line contract
Program receives a single .asm filename and writes a .hack file with 16-bit lines.
  1. Accept single command-line argument: input .asm file.
  2. Produce output file with .hack extension, same base name.
  3. Write one 16-character string of 0s and 1s per instruction line.
  4. Handle A-instructions, C-instructions, labels, and variables.
Check
Run: assembler Prog.asm → produces Prog.hack; inspect file length and a few sample lines to confirm format.
Common CLI mistakes
  • • Not trimming comments and blank lines, shifting ROM addresses.
  • • Writing binary lines with wrong width or missing leading zeros.
  • • Failing to create output file if path handling is incorrect.
Try this
Run your assembler on Add.asm and compare Add.hack to the reference before proceeding to more complex tests.

screens.title: Parser, SymbolTable, and Code modules
screens.narratorSegment: The assembler is cleanly decomposed into three modules: Parser, SymbolTable, and Code. The Parser reads the input file line by line, strips comments and whitespace, and exposes the current instruction type and fields: for A-instructions it provides the symbol or number, for C-instructions it yields dest, comp, and jump parts, and for label declarations it yields the symbol. The SymbolTable stores mappings from symbols to addresses; it starts preloaded with predefined symbols and grows during the first and second passes when labels and variables are discovered. The Code module encapsulates the translation tables: given mnemonic strings it returns the bit patterns for comp, dest, and jump. This separation helps testing: you can unit-test Code translations independently, verify SymbolTable lookups separately, and test the Parser on various formatting styles. A common design error is scattering symbol logic across modules; keep SymbolTable responsible only for mapping names to addresses. A useful mental model is three collaborators: Parser supplies structured data, SymbolTable stores names, Code returns bit encodings. When implemented, you can run fast, focused tests and replace one module without rewriting the others.

keyIdea.text: Parser breaks lines into fields, SymbolTable maps names to addresses, and Code converts mnemonics to bit strings.

content.html:
Module 4 › Architecture › Modules
Module responsibilities
Parser
Cleans lines, identifies instruction type, extracts symbol or dest/comp/jump fields for each instruction.
SymbolTable
Stores symbol → address mappings, preloads predefined symbols, supports add and contains operations.
Code
Holds comp/dest/jump translation tables and returns fixed-width bit strings for each mnemonic.
Testing strategy
  • Unit-test Code mappings to ensure each mnemonic maps to the correct bits.
  • Feed sample lines to Parser to verify whitespace and comment handling.
  • Verify SymbolTable add/get semantics and initial predefined entries.
Design tip
Keep symbol resolution logic in SymbolTable and keep Parser focused on structure. This reduces bugs where addressing is accidentally computed twice.
Why this helps
Modular code simplifies debugging and allows isolated unit tests for each concern.

screens.title: Parser: reading and classifying lines
screens.narratorSegment: The Parser's job is straightforward but requires care. It must read each line, remove whitespace and comments, and then classify the instruction as A-instruction, C-instruction, or label. A typical approach is to ignore lines that become empty after stripping comments. For an A-instruction like at-sign followed by symbols or digits, the parser yields the symbol part; for C-instructions it splits around equals and semicolon to extract dest, comp, and jump fields. A common mistake is not handling lines with only comments or trailing spaces; this shifts ROM addresses when labels are recorded. Here's a short Python-style outline you can adapt: read lines into a list, iterate while skipping blank lines, on each non-empty line determine the type, and expose accessor methods like instruction_type(), symbol(), dest(), comp(), and jump(). Unit-test the parser with edge cases: leading/trailing whitespace, lines with only comments, and variations of C-instruction formatting. A final sanity check is that the count of instructions seen in the parser during the first pass equals the number of binary lines you write in the second pass. How will your parser handle tabs and mixed whitespace?

keyIdea.title: Parser reliability
keyIdea.text: Correct parsing requires consistent handling of whitespace, comments, and instruction decomposition to avoid address shifts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Parser › Code Walkthrough
Parsing steps
  1. Open and read the input .asm file into lines.
  2. Strip comments (text after //) and trim whitespace.
  3. Skip empty lines.
  4. Classify instructions and extract fields with accessor methods.
def advance():
  line = next_raw_line()
  line = remove_comment(line).strip()
  if not line: continue
  if line.startswith('('): type = 'L_INSTRUCTION'
  elif line.startswith('@'): type = 'A_INSTRUCTION'
  else: type = 'C_INSTRUCTION'
Examples to test
  • • Leading tabs and spaces mixed with code.
  • • Lines like "D=M // comment" that include inline comments.
  • • Label lines such as "(LOOP)" that must not increment ROM address.
Misconception
Skipping comment removal is easy to miss and leads to wrong ROM addresses because labels are recorded for the next actual instruction.

screens.title: SymbolTable and variables
screens.narratorSegment: Symbol management is central to the assembler. The SymbolTable begins prepopulated with predefined symbols such as screen, keyboard, and general-purpose registers (these are specified in the course materials). During the first pass you add label symbols when you encounter a (LABEL) declaration, mapping that label to the ROM address of the next instruction. During the second pass you handle variables: when an A-instruction contains a non-numeric symbol and it is not already in the symbol table, allocate the next available R A M address starting at 16 and record it. A concrete example: encountering @i where i is first used in the program causes the assembler to assign R A M[16] to i, then later references to @i use that address. A common bug is starting variable allocation from the wrong address or failing to add labels during the first pass, producing incorrect address resolution. To avoid errors, keep the rules separated: first pass only records labels and ROM addresses, second pass only assigns variable R A M addresses as needed. The learning checkpoint is to explain how a forward reference — using a label before it appears — is handled safely by this two-pass approach.

keyIdea.title: Two kinds of symbols
keyIdea.text: Labels map to ROM addresses found in the first pass; variables are allocated in RAM starting at address 16 during the second pass when first referenced.

content.html:
Module 4 › Symbols › SymbolTable
Symbol categories
  • • Predefined symbols: constants and memory-mapped I/O addresses supplied by the spec.
  • • Labels: declared with parentheses; give a ROM address for the next instruction.
  • • Variables: user-defined names assigned RAM addresses starting at 16 on first use.
Rule
First pass records label → ROM address. Second pass assigns variables when encountered, starting from 16.
Concrete scenario
If the code uses a symbol @count before you see a label (LOOP), two-pass ensures count is either a predefined symbol, a previously allocated variable, or assigned now. If you used a single pass, forward label references could not be resolved without complex backpatching.
Common bug
Off-by-one when recording label addresses: labels label the next instruction, not the line containing the label itself.

screens.title: Translating C-instructions
screens.narratorSegment: C-instructions are the trickiest translation because they contain three fields: dest, comp, and jump. The assembler uses the Code module to map each mnemonic to a fixed-width bit string: comp maps to a 7-bit or 6-bit pattern depending on whether the A register or M memory is referenced, dest maps to three bits indicating which registers are written, and jump maps to three bits that control program flow. The full machine encoding for a C-instruction begins with the bits 111 followed by comp, dest, and jump fields. A concrete example: given the assembly D=M, the parser yields dest="D", comp="M", and jump="". Code. comp("M") returns the comp bits that select memory as the operand, Code. dest("D") returns 010 and Code. jump("") returns 000, so the final line written is 111 + compBits + destBits + jumpBits. A common misconception is to forget the 111 prefix or to swap dest and jump bit positions. Always consult the exact bit layout and unit-test each Code mapping. A final check is to assemble a handful of known C-instructions and verify their binary outputs match references.

keyIdea.text: A C-instruction is encoded as 111 followed by comp bits, dest bits, and jump bits; accurate tables and tests prevent bit-order bugs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Translation › C-instructions
Encoding pattern
C-instruction → 111 comp(7) dest(3) jump(3)
Example walkthrough
Assembly: D=M
111 [compBits for M] [010] [000]
Testing tips
  • • Unit-test Code.comp on each mnemonic, including A vs M variants.
  • • Unit-test Code.dest for all dest combinations like MD, AM, AMD.
  • • Test jump encodings for JEQ, JGT, JLE, etc., and empty jump equals 000.
Misconception
Swapping dest and jump fields or forgetting the 111 prefix will produce invalid machine instructions that the Hack CPU will not execute as intended.

screens.title: First pass and label resolution
screens.narratorSegment: The first pass over the cleaned input lines builds the symbol table for labels. Walk through the file, keep a ROM address counter initialized to zero, and for each non-label instruction increment that counter. When you encounter a label declaration like (LOOP), record symbol_table. add_entry('LOOP', rom_address) but do not increment the counter for that line. This ensures that the label maps to the address of the next actual instruction. A common off-by-one bug happens when implementers increment the ROM counter on label lines or include commented lines in the count. Test your first pass by running it on a program with several labels and checking that the stored addresses correspond to expected instruction indices. This pass must not allocate variables; only record labels and predefined symbols. The reason for a dedicated first pass is to support forward references: when the second pass encounters @LOOP before (LOOP) appears, the label will already be recorded and the correct address used. Can you find a small test program where a forward reference would fail in a single-pass assembler? First pass and label resolution means record label → rom address mappings without emitting machine code, ensuring forward label references resolve in the second pass.. In practical terms, record labels so forward references work. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Two-Pass › First Pass
First pass: label collection
Scan cleaned instructions, increment ROM addresses for concrete instructions, and add label symbols without incrementing.
Algorithm
  1. rom_address = 0
  2. For each line: if label → add_entry(symbol, rom_address)
  3. Else → rom_address += 1
Quick test
Write a short program with two labels and three instructions; assert recorded addresses match indices of the instructions that follow the labels.
Key Takeaway

The first pass does not emit code; it only records label addresses so forward references are resolvable in the second pass.

screens.title: Second pass: translating and allocating variables
screens.narratorSegment: During the second pass you reset the parser and iterate through the cleaned instruction stream again to emit machine code. Maintain a ram_address counter starting at 16 for the first variable you assign. For each A-instruction: if its symbol is a decimal number, convert that number to a 16-bit binary string and write it. If it is a symbol, consult the SymbolTable: if it exists, use its address; otherwise add it with ram_address and increment ram_address. content.html:
Module 4 › Emission › Second Pass
Second pass steps
  1. Reset parser; set ram_address = 16.
  2. For each A-instruction: if numeric → write binary; else lookup/allocate symbol then write address in binary.
  3. For each C-instruction: compute comp/dest/jump bits and write 111 + bits.
# writing an A-instruction
if symbol.isdigit(): address = int(symbol)
else:
  if not symbol_table.contains(symbol):
    symbol_table.add_entry(symbol, ram_address)
    ram_address += 1
  address = symbol_table.get_address(symbol)
out.write(f"{address:016b}
")
Pitfall and check
Ensure ram_address begins at 16 and that predefined symbols are present to avoid collisions. After writing the file, check total lines equal the number of non-label instructions encountered in the first pass.
Misconception
Allocating variables in the first pass or including labels as instructions will produce wrong addresses; separation of passes prevents this.

screens.title: Testing strategy: Add to Pong
screens.narratorSegment: Testing your assembler progressively is the fastest path to correctness. Start with Add. asm: a small program that verifies basic A- and C-instructions. If Add passes, move to Max. asm to test conditional jumps and labels. Next, run Rect. asm to exercise variables and screen memory addressing. Finally, assemble Pong. asm as a stress test; Pong will reveal issues that smaller tests hide: large symbol tables, many variables, complex C-instruction permutations, and forward references in many places. When a mismatch occurs, use a line-by-line diff to find the first incorrect binary line. Decode that line back into instruction fields: is it A or C? If A, was the resolved address correct? If C, check comp/dest/jump encodings and verify Code tables. Common debugging steps include printing intermediate parser output, dumping the symbol table contents, and asserting that the number of emitted lines matches the first pass count. Keep automated tests that run your assembler against provided. asm files and compare outputs; this saves time as you iterate. After debugging, write a brief note describing the bug and how you fixed it so you remember the lesson for the future.

screens.title: Why the assembler matters
screens.narratorSegment: The assembler is small but conceptually powerful. It demonstrates that programs can manipulate programs: your assembler reads an assembly program and produces a machine program. This idea underpins compilers, interpreters, and toolchains. A practical significance is cross-compilation: your assembler runs on your laptop architecture and produces code for the Hack architecture. This separation allows development on one platform while targeting another. Comparing the assembler to later compiler projects, notice that the assembler performs a direct one-to-one translation without optimization, while compilers introduce more complex analyses and multiple translation stages. A helpful reflection exercise is to ask what would need to change to make the assembler a single-pass tool: you would need a strategy to resolve forward references, such as backpatching or reserving space, which complicates the implementation. The next logical step after building an assembler is to build a compiler that translates a high-level language into assembly; that will require syntax trees, symbol scopes, and code generation strategies. As you conclude this project, take a moment to write down the most surprising bug you fixed and why it taught you about building reliable tools.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Remember three core ideas from the assembler project. First, the two-pass strategy: use the first pass to record label addresses and the second pass to emit machine code and allocate variables. This clean separation avoids forward-reference confusion. Second, modular design: separate Parser, SymbolTable, and Code so you can test and reason about each piece; keep symbol allocation in one place and encoding tables in another. Third, progressive testing: start with Add, advance to Max and Rect, and use Pong as a stress test to reveal subtle bugs like wrong variable allocation or incorrect comp encodings. These concepts are small but foundational: they teach how to build reliable translator tools and prepare you for compiler work. Keep these in mind when you debug, explain your fixes, and plan the next projects.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build an assembler that reads Hack assembly language and produces Hack machine code. This is the first software project in the course and it matters because you will write a program that creates programs — a small but powerful form of compilation. The assembler accepts a. asm file, resolves labels and variables, and writes a. hack file with 16-bit binary instructions. Practically speaking, you will implement a parser to break each line into instruction fields, a symbol table to map names to addresses, and a code module to translate mnemonics into bit patterns. You will test on small programs like Add and larger stress tests like Pong, which reveals subtle bugs that small tests miss. By completing this project you learn how human-readable instructions map to machine-level encodings and why two passes—one to record labels and one to translate instructions—are a reliable approach. Think about how a program that writes programs changes your role: you become a builder of tools that create behavior on different hardware. What will your assembler reveal when you run Pong?

These learning objectives guide the work you will do while implementing the assembler. First, you will complete Project 5 by producing a working assembler that accepts a. asm file and emits a. hack file formatted as 16-bit binary lines. Second, you will test that assembler against provided programs to validate correctness, from simple Add programs to the complex Pong game. Third, you will understand how assembly language relates to machine code: how symbols, addresses, and instruction fields map to bit patterns. Fourth, you will reflect on building a program that manipulates other programs, recognizing why the assembler is a simple compiler and why that matters for cross-compilation and layered toolchains. Each objective is practical: implementing, testing, reasoning, and reflecting. You will demonstrate competency by running your assembler on all course examples and explaining how label resolution and variable allocation work in your code.

In addition to the code you write, verification is essential. Learn how to compare your assembler's output against reference. hack files line-by-line and how to interpret mismatches. You will learn to trace differences by mapping a binary line back to the original assembly: locate the instruction, check symbol resolution, and confirm comp/dest/jump encodings. This objective teaches practical debugging habits: isolate whether a mismatch stems from label address off-by-one, variable allocation starting address, missing predefined symbols, or incorrect parsing of whitespace and comments. Being able to explain why a failing test fails is the difference between a passing run and a robust tool. You will also learn to document the modules in your assembler and to present a short report showing tests passed, remaining issues, and the strategies used to find bugs.

An assembler is a program that converts assembly language into machine code. For Project 5 you will implement a Hack assembler that reads human-readable mnemonics and symbolic names and writes 16-bit binary instructions the Hack C P U can execute. Conceptually, the assembler maps textual constructs to fixed-width encodings: an A-instruction becomes a single 16-bit value with the high bit zero and the address in the remaining bits; a C-instruction is encoded with a three-bit prefix, a comp field, dest bits, and jump bits. This translation is precise and unforgiving: a single wrong bit changes behavior. A concrete example is an A-instruction with a numeric address like @17, which should become the 16-bit binary representation of 17. A common misconception is that an assembler merely performs text replacement; instead it must parse, resolve symbols, allocate addresses for variables, and consult translation tables for comp/dest/jump. The key takeaway is that the assembler is the simplest compiler: it implements lexical and syntactic recognition at a small scale and produces exact bit patterns. When you finish this module, ask yourself: how does your symbol resolution strategy ensure labels point to the correct ROM address?

Project 5 specifies a simple but exact interface: your assembler must accept a single command-line argument — the name of a. asm file — and produce an output file with the same base name and a. hack extension. Each line in the output file represents a single 16-bit instruction as a string of 0s and 1s. Why this matters: strict input/output contracts let test harnesses run your program automatically and compare outputs precisely. A common execution pattern is to invoke the assembler with a program name, open the. asm file, then write lines to the. hack file in order. A frequent pitfall is not handling file naming edge cases or failing to strip comments and blank lines before translation, which shifts ROM addresses. A concrete practice is to run your assembler on Add. asm and compare the produced Add. hack line-for-line with the reference. If the first differing line is at address 10, trace how you computed addresses up to that point. Remember that the spec requires handling A-instructions, C-instructions, labels, and variables. Before moving on, confirm your program opens files, iterates clean lines, and writes 16-character binary strings for every instruction.

The assembler is cleanly decomposed into three modules: Parser, SymbolTable, and Code. The Parser reads the input file line by line, strips comments and whitespace, and exposes the current instruction type and fields: for A-instructions it provides the symbol or number, for C-instructions it yields dest, comp, and jump parts, and for label declarations it yields the symbol. The SymbolTable stores mappings from symbols to addresses; it starts preloaded with predefined symbols and grows during the first and second passes when labels and variables are discovered. The Code module encapsulates the translation tables: given mnemonic strings it returns the bit patterns for comp, dest, and jump. This separation helps testing: you can unit-test Code translations independently, verify SymbolTable lookups separately, and test the Parser on various formatting styles. A common design error is scattering symbol logic across modules; keep SymbolTable responsible only for mapping names to addresses. A useful mental model is three collaborators: Parser supplies structured data, SymbolTable stores names, Code returns bit encodings. When implemented, you can run fast, focused tests and replace one module without rewriting the others.

The Parser's job is straightforward but requires care. It must read each line, remove whitespace and comments, and then classify the instruction as A-instruction, C-instruction, or label. A typical approach is to ignore lines that become empty after stripping comments. For an A-instruction like at-sign followed by symbols or digits, the parser yields the symbol part; for C-instructions it splits around equals and semicolon to extract dest, comp, and jump fields. A common mistake is not handling lines with only comments or trailing spaces; this shifts ROM addresses when labels are recorded. Here's a short Python-style outline you can adapt: read lines into a list, iterate while skipping blank lines, on each non-empty line determine the type, and expose accessor methods like instruction_type(), symbol(), dest(), comp(), and jump(). Unit-test the parser with edge cases: leading/trailing whitespace, lines with only comments, and variations of C-instruction formatting. A final sanity check is that the count of instructions seen in the parser during the first pass equals the number of binary lines you write in the second pass. How will your parser handle tabs and mixed whitespace?

Symbol management is central to the assembler. The SymbolTable begins prepopulated with predefined symbols such as screen, keyboard, and general-purpose registers (these are specified in the course materials). During the first pass you add label symbols when you encounter a (LABEL) declaration, mapping that label to the ROM address of the next instruction. During the second pass you handle variables: when an A-instruction contains a non-numeric symbol and it is not already in the symbol table, allocate the next available R A M address starting at 16 and record it. A concrete example: encountering @i where i is first used in the program causes the assembler to assign R A M[16] to i, then later references to @i use that address. A common bug is starting variable allocation from the wrong address or failing to add labels during the first pass, producing incorrect address resolution. To avoid errors, keep the rules separated: first pass only records labels and ROM addresses, second pass only assigns variable R A M addresses as needed. The learning checkpoint is to explain how a forward reference — using a label before it appears — is handled safely by this two-pass approach.

C-instructions are the trickiest translation because they contain three fields: dest, comp, and jump. The assembler uses the Code module to map each mnemonic to a fixed-width bit string: comp maps to a 7-bit or 6-bit pattern depending on whether the A register or M memory is referenced, dest maps to three bits indicating which registers are written, and jump maps to three bits that control program flow. The full machine encoding for a C-instruction begins with the bits 111 followed by comp, dest, and jump fields. A concrete example: given the assembly D=M, the parser yields dest="D", comp="M", and jump="". Code. comp("M") returns the comp bits that select memory as the operand, Code. dest("D") returns 010 and Code. jump("") returns 000, so the final line written is 111 + compBits + destBits + jumpBits. A common misconception is to forget the 111 prefix or to swap dest and jump bit positions. Always consult the exact bit layout and unit-test each Code mapping. A final check is to assemble a handful of known C-instructions and verify their binary outputs match references.

The first pass over the cleaned input lines builds the symbol table for labels. Walk through the file, keep a ROM address counter initialized to zero, and for each non-label instruction increment that counter. When you encounter a label declaration like (LOOP), record symbol_table. add_entry('LOOP', rom_address) but do not increment the counter for that line. This ensures that the label maps to the address of the next actual instruction. A common off-by-one bug happens when implementers increment the ROM counter on label lines or include commented lines in the count. Test your first pass by running it on a program with several labels and checking that the stored addresses correspond to expected instruction indices. This pass must not allocate variables; only record labels and predefined symbols. The reason for a dedicated first pass is to support forward references: when the second pass encounters @LOOP before (LOOP) appears, the label will already be recorded and the correct address used.
